hints: Think about how a neutral $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecule can be polarised to release $\text{Cl}^{+}$, a strong Lewis acid that accepts a lone pair from chlorine works well here.
walkthrough:
Make chlorine electrophilic enough to attack benzene**
Benzene is electron rich but its delocalised ring is very stable, so neutral $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is not electrophilic enough on its own. You need a Lewis acid that pulls electron density away from $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to generate the powerful electrophile $\text{Cl}^{+}$.

Choose the standard halogen carrier**
$\text{AlCl}_{3}$ accepts a lone pair from $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to form $\text{AlCl}_{4}^{-}$ plus $\text{Cl}^{+}$. That $\text{Cl}^{+}$ then attacks the benzene ring. $\text{FeCl}_{3}$ behaves similarly, but $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ is the classic answer here.

hints: Look at where arrow x starts in diagram 1, inside the benzene ring, and ask what electron source in benzene attacks an electrophile.
Follow where arrow x points, to the $\text{Cl}^{+}$ ion, and ask what new covalent bond must appear in diagram 2 as a result.
walkthrough:
Read arrow x as benzene acting as a nucleophile**
Arrow x starts from the circle in diagram 1. That circle is shorthand for the six delocalised $\pi$ electrons above and below the ring. A pair from that delocalised system is donated toward the $\text{Cl}^{+}$ electrophile.

See the new sigma bond that forms**
When that $\pi$ pair is used to bond to $\text{Cl}^{+}$, the aromaticity is temporarily broken. In diagram 2 you now have a $\text{C-Cl}$ sigma bond at the top right carbon. So that same electron pair is now localised in the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond.

Final answer: Before step 1: in the delocalised $\pi$ system / delocalised ring of benzene.
After step 1: in the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond (of the intermediate in diagram 2).

hints: Look at where arrow y starts in diagram 2, from the $\text{C-H}$ region back into the ring, and think which bond must break to restore aromaticity.
Consider what makes chlorobenzene in diagram 3 so stable again, and where the returning electron pair must end up.
walkthrough:
Spot the bond that must break in step 2**
In diagram 2 the ring has lost its full delocalisation. To get it back, the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the substituted carbon breaks. Arrow y shows that $\text{C-H}$ bonding pair moving back into the ring, with $\text{H}^{+}$ leaving.

Restore the aromatic sextet**
Once that pair returns to the ring, all six carbons share six $\pi$ electrons again. In diagram 3 the circle is redrawn, showing the pair is now part of the delocalised $\pi$ system of chlorobenzene.

Final answer: Before step 2: in the $\text{C-H}$ bond (at the same carbon as the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond).
After step 2: in the delocalised $\pi$ system / delocalised ring of chlorobenzene.

hints: In diagram 2, find the one carbon bonded to four groups ($\text{H}$, $\text{Cl}$ and two ring $\text{C}$ atoms) and recall its geometry and hybridisation.
walkthrough:
Count geometries in the intermediate**
Picture diagram 2. Five carbons are still trigonal planar with three sigma bonds each, so they remain $sp^{2}$. The carbon carrying both $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cl}$ has four sigma bonds and tetrahedral geometry, so it has become $sp^{3}$. No carbon is linear, so $sp$ count is $0$. That gives $0$, $5$, $1$.

Final answer: sp hybridised: 0
sp$^{2}$ hybridised: 5
sp$^{3}$ hybridised: 1

hints: Remember benzene keeps its ring and only swaps one $\text{H}$ for one $\text{Cl}$, so think what the second chlorine atom from $\text{Cl}_{2}$ combines with.
walkthrough:
Balance as substitution**
One $\text{Cl}$ from $\text{Cl}_{2}$ replaces one $\text{H}$ on benzene to give chlorobenzene, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$. The displaced $\text{H}$ joins the other $\text{Cl}$ to give $\text{HCl}$. So: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6} + \text{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$$

hints: Recall which positively charged species attacks the ring in step 1, and which atom leaves the ring in step 2.
walkthrough:
Fill the sentence logically**
The species attracted to the electron rich ring is $\text{Cl}^{+}$, so that is the electrophile. In the product the ring has lost $\text{H}$ and gained $\text{Cl}$, so a hydrogen atom is substituted by a chlorine atom.
Final answer: During this reaction, the electrophile is $\text{Cl}^{+}$ and a hydrogen / $\text{H}$ atom in benzene is substituted by a chlorine / $\text{Cl}$ atom.

hints: Think about the standard reaction of a primary chloroalkane with warm aqueous alkali and what $\text{OH}^{-}$ replaces.
walkthrough:
Link chloroethane to alcohol formation**
$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ undergoes nucleophilic substitution by $\text{OH}^{-}$. The $\text{Cl}$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$ to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, ethanol.

Final answer: mechanism: nucleophilic substitution
major organic product: ethanol

hints: Compare the environment of $\text{Cl}$ in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ with that in $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$, and ask how a p orbital on $\text{Cl}$ can overlap with the benzene $\pi$ system.
Think about how that overlap changes the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond order and strength, and why $\text{OH}^{-}$ cannot easily break it.
walkthrough:
See the extra interaction only chlorobenzene has**
In chloroethane the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is a simple single sigma bond. In chlorobenzene one of the $3p$ lone pairs on $\text{Cl}$ can overlap sideways with the delocalised $\pi$ system of the ring. This delocalisation pulls electron density into the $\text{C-Cl}$ region.

Explain why the bond resists attack**
That overlap gives the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character, making it shorter and stronger than the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in chloroethane. Nucleophilic attack by $\text{OH}^{-}$ would require breaking this strong bond and disrupting aromaticity, so no reaction occurs under these conditions.

Final answer: A lone pair on $\text{Cl}$ in chlorobenzene is delocalised / overlaps with the $\pi$ system of the ring.
The $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in chlorobenzene is stronger / has partial double bond character, so is not broken by $\text{NaOH(aq)}$.
